title: Free providers and agents
text:
This page lists the free ways to run the course exercises: the agents you type commands into, and the providers that supply the model behind them. Read Standard setup first for the base installation.
Written for: learners choosing their first agent, and volunteers who need to explain the options.

title: Free providers and agents
text:
1. Choose by your situation
Answer these questions first. The rows point to the options that usually fit.



Your situation
Good starting point




You are new to the terminal and want a visual window
Cline or Continue in VS Code


You are comfortable in the terminal and want to see every step
Gemini CLI or Aider


You want one account that unlocks many free models
OpenRouter as the model source


You have no card and only a Google login
Gemini CLI with your Google account


Your data is sensitive and must stay on your machine
A local model through Ollama, with Aider, Cline or OpenCode pointed at it


You want an open-source agent you can read and change
OpenCode or Aider


Your work laptop blocks installs
The browser-only path in Standard setup



You can change your choice later. Your project files and AGENTS.md do not depend on the agent you used to write them.

title: Free providers and agents
section: 2. The two layers: agent and model
text:
2. The two layers: agent and model
Every option has two parts, and it helps to keep them separate in your head:

The agent is the program you run. It reads your files, proposes edits and runs commands. Examples: Gemini CLI, Aider, Cline, OpenCode.
The model is the AI that does the thinking. It is supplied by a provider, such as Google, OpenRouter or a model running on your own computer.

Some agents only work with one provider (Gemini CLI works with Google). Others accept many providers (Aider, Cline and OpenCode accept OpenRouter and most others). Using an agent that accepts many providers gives you the most options if one provider runs out of free quota.

title: Free providers and agents
text:
3. The agents

Gemini CLI (Google)
A terminal agent from Google. It is the default for the course exercises.



Runs in
Terminal


Install
npm install -g @google/gemini-cli (needs Node.js, see Standard setup)


Sign-in
Your Google account, the first time you run gemini


Free limit (Google login, reported)
About 1,000 model requests per day and 60 per minute


Free limit (unpaid API key, reported)
About 250 requests per day and 10 per minute, Flash models only


Best for
Learners who want the fewest steps and no API key


Watch out for
The free tier and product name may change. Some reports say Gemini CLI is moving to Antigravity CLI. Check the official site before you rely on it.



Start it from your project folder with gemini. The first run asks you to sign in.


Aider (open source)
A terminal agent that works with almost any model. It edits your files directly and can commit each change to Git.







Runs in
Terminal


Install (official route)
python -m pip install aider-install, then run aider-install


Install (uv route)
uv tool install aider-chat


Key
An OpenRouter key, or a Google key, set as an environment variable


Best for
Learners who want to see every change and control the model directly


Watch out for
You choose the model yourself. Model names must be written exactly, for example openrouter/<provider>/<model>.



To use a free OpenRouter model, put the key in .env, then run:
aider --model openrouter/qwen/qwen3-coder:free
To see what is available, run aider --list-models openrouter/.


Cline (VS Code)
A free extension for VS Code with a visual panel. You bring your own key and pay the model provider, which can be zero on a free tier.







Runs in
VS Code


Install
VS Code Extensions panel, then search “Cline”


Key
OpenRouter key entered in Cline’s settings


Best for
Learners who are not yet comfortable in the terminal (Builder track)


Watch out for
The extension is free, but the model is not. Check the price of each model. Set a spending limit on your key.



In Cline’s settings, pick OpenRouter as the provider and paste your key. For free models, search the dropdown for “free”, or choose openrouter/free, which picks a free model for each request.


Continue (VS Code)
An open-source VS Code extension that works like Cline and accepts many providers. It is useful if you want a second option that runs inside the editor. Setup is similar to Cline: pick a provider and paste the key.


OpenCode (open source)
An open-source terminal agent that connects to many providers, including local models through Ollama. Sources report that it includes free models that work without an account, though the list rotates.



Runs in
Terminal


Install
brew install opencode (macOS or Linux with Homebrew), or npm install -g opencode-ai


Windows
Use WSL, as in Standard setup


Start
Go to your project folder and run opencode


Key
Optional for built-in free models; needed for OpenRouter or Google


Best for
Learners who want an open-source agent and may later use local models


Watch out for
Free models change without notice. Check the official docs (opencode.ai) for the current list.

title: Free providers and agents
text:
4. The providers

Google Gemini
Two ways to get free Gemini access:

Google login through Gemini CLI. No key needed. This is the simplest route and what the course default uses.
An API key from Google AI Studio. Free, no card required for the basic tier. Use it with Aider, Cline, OpenCode or any agent that accepts a Google key. Store it in .env as shown in Standard setup.

Free limits are per day and per minute, and they change. The unpaid API key allows far fewer requests than the Google login route.


OpenRouter
OpenRouter gives one account and one key for many models. Free models have IDs ending in :free.



Sign-up
https://openrouter.ai, create a key at the Keys page


Card
Not needed for free models


Limits (reported)
20 requests per minute. Daily limit is reported as 50 requests on the unfunded tier, and some sources say 200. Buying about USD 10 in credits raises the daily limit to 1,000. Check the current figure on openrouter.ai.


Model list
Changes often. Free models can be busy at peak hours and disappear without notice.


Data
Whether prompts are kept or used for training depends on the provider serving each model. Check the model’s page before sending anything sensitive.



Good first models to try are the ones marked :free on the model page. Some agents let you list fallback models, so that if one is busy another answers.


Local models (Ollama)
For private work, run a small model on your own computer. Nothing leaves your machine, but results are weaker and slower than hosted models. Use it for sensitive exercises only after a short test. Install Ollama from https://ollama.com, pull a small coding model, and point Aider, Cline or OpenCode at the local endpoint. Most learners with 8–16 GB RAM can run a model of about 1.5–8 billion parameters.

title: Free providers and agents
text:
6. Record your choice
Write your choice in your project’s AGENTS.md, so the agent and your teammates know which tools you use:
# Tool choice

- Agent: Gemini CLI (Google login)
- Fallback agent: Aider with OpenRouter model `openrouter/qwen/qwen3-coder:free`
- Private work: none; do not use hosted tools for private data
Re-check the limits and model names before each session. The sources used for this page were gathered in October 2026, and free tiers change often.

title: Agentic Software Development & Vibe Coding Training Series — Roadmap Synthesis
text:
UNDP Istanbul International Center for Private Sector in Development (IICPSD) · UN Volunteer trainers


This roadmap focused for researchers and early-career professionals, from Least Developed Countries and developing economies from no prior experience with AI coding agents to shipping a small, tested and deployed product. It is built around the real constraints of this audience, especially no GPU, no paid AI subscriptions and unreliable connectivity.



Starting point: the learner may never have used a terminal, Git or an AI coding agent, and may have no GPU and no paid AI subscription.
By the end of the series, every learner should be able to:

Use a terminal, Git and GitHub to create, version and share a project.
Tell apart chat, vibe coding and agentic engineering, and explain what an LLM, an augmented LLM, a workflow and an agent are.
Recognise hallucination, insecure code and technical debt in AI output, and apply basic data-privacy rules.
Choose a tool path (zero-cost, balanced, premium or private/local) using its cost, safety and effort.
Configure a coding agent, keep secrets out of code and write a project rules file.
Turn a real business need into a specification and drive an agent from it.
Explain the plan-act-observe loop, implement tool calling and set permissions with human approval.
Judge when a multi-agent setup is worth using, and run one safely.
Turn acceptance criteria into automated tests, CI checks and simple evals.
Audit, debug and roll back AI-generated code.
Manage context for large codebases and for small local models.
Deploy a project from CI to a live URL, with secrets, logging and cost control.
Deliver a capstone micro-product with a spec, tests, CI, a README and a demo.

The guiding rule from the meeting still applies: every graduate should be efficient in at least one area, not superficially aware of all of them. All learners follow the same roadmap.



The following design decision were taken from the alignment meeting of UNV.
One roadmap, not a list of lectures. Every session is a learning component on a shared path from point A to point B (Alan).
Shared vocabulary first. Session 1 defines LLM, augmented LLM, workflow and agent once, and every trainer uses those terms the same way (Alan).
A ladder with less repetition, but friendly to drop-ins. Each concept has one owning session. Later sessions open with a three-to-five-minute recap and a link to the owning recording rather than re-teaching it.
Depth over breadth. The series teaches the top three or four tools in each category in depth, instead of skimming the whole ecosystem.
Real workflows, with notebooks as companions. Practice happens in the terminal, the IDE and Git, because that is how agentic coding is done in practice. Notebooks, which the ToR lists among supporting materials, accompany the sessions where they genuinely help, such as building an agent loop or running evals.
Explicit cost, safety and effort paths. Learners choose between zero-cost, balanced, premium and private/local paths with their trade-offs spelled out (Alan, Akshi).
Privacy by default. Private, personal or organizational data never goes into external AI tools. Exercises use synthetic or public data, and sensitive work uses local models (Ruiya).
Horizontal expertise. Volunteers bring different niches, such as geospatial data science, workflow automation with self-hosted n8n (Seth), UN IT practice and solution architecture. Sessions can include short expert spotlights, and session length is flexible around a 60-minute target (Emanuel).
The zero-cost guarantee. Every exercise and the capstone must be completable with an ordinary laptop or a browser and no paid tools. Premium tools can be demonstrated, but every demo also shows the free equivalent.













Path
Examples
Cost
Safety
Effort




Zero-cost (default for exercises)
Aider, Cline or Continue with free API tiers; Gemini CLI; GitHub Copilot Free; GitHub Codespaces; self-hosted n8n
USD 0
Medium: free tiers may use prompts for training
Medium


Balanced
Pay-as-you-go API key with a spending cap; one entry-level IDE agent plan; n8n on a cheap server
About USD 5–20 per month
Medium to high
Low to medium


Premium (demo only)
Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, paid Cursor or Windsurf
USD 20+ per month
High on enterprise plans
Low


Private / local
Ollama or LM Studio with small quantized coding models
USD 0 software, hardware-bound
Highest
High



Free tiers and prices change often, so every free-tier option must be re-checked the week before the session that uses it.



The path has four phases: Foundation, Core Mechanics, Quality & Scale, and Ship. Every live session follows the same template: entry recap, objectives, concept, live demo (premium tool plus its free equivalent), real-world use case, hands-on exercise, and deliverable.











#
Session
Phase
What learners will be able to do
Real-world use case
Deliverable




0
Onboarding & command-line survival kit (async)
Foundation
Use a terminal, Git and GitHub; set up VS Code or a browser Codespace; store an API key safely
Setting up a reproducible workspace for a team project
Passing environment check and a pushed “hello-agent” repo


1
Introduction to the vibe paradigm
Foundation
Place chat, vibe coding and agentic engineering on a spectrum; tell an LLM, augmented LLM, workflow and agent apart; spot hallucination, insecure code and technical debt; apply privacy rules
A one-page tool for a local cooperative, built three ways and compared
Small working artifact and a short critique


2
Architecting & configuring the AI workspace
Foundation
Choose a tool path with a cost, safety and effort matrix; configure an agent with a free or local model; manage secrets; write a project rules file
Choosing a setup for an NGO that cannot send data to external services
Working workspace and a committed AGENTS.md


3
Development paradigms
Core Mechanics
Choose between vibe iteration, spec-driven development and orchestration; turn a business requirement into a spec; drive an agent from it
A market-price tracker or a clinic queue page specified from a real need
spec.md and its implementation (reused in later sessions)


4
Agentic mechanics: planning & tool use
Core Mechanics
Explain the plan-act-observe loop; implement tool calling; understand MCP; set permissions and human approvals
An assistant that looks up data and drafts a weekly report
Mini agent or n8n workflow with a logged run; companion notebook


5
Managing multi-agent teams
Core Mechanics
Use orchestrator-worker and planner-coder-reviewer patterns; run agents in parallel safely; judge when multi-agent setups are not worth it
Splitting a feature for a small business website across agents
Pipeline with reviewer output on a real change


6
The safety net: automated validation & evals
Quality & Scale
Turn acceptance criteria into tests; add linting and security checks; set up CI; write simple evals for LLM features
Making sure a public-service form never accepts invalid data
Passing CI and at least five meaningful tests; companion eval notebook


7
Debugging in the agentic age
Quality & Scale
Audit AI-generated code; give agents good error context; escape the “fix loop”; roll back with Git; refactor technical debt
Fixing a broken AI-built donation page
Bug report and fix with regression tests


8
Context engineering & large codebases
Quality & Scale
Manage the context window; build a context pack; use docs and code search to cut hallucinations; adapt to small local models
Contributing to an existing open-source civic-tech project
Context pack and a scoped pull request


9
AI-first SDLC: deployment & operations
Ship
Deploy from CI to a free host; handle production secrets, logging and monitoring; control API costs; plan rollbacks
Putting the session 3 project online for real users
Public URL and deployment workflow


10
Capstone: an autonomous micro-product
Ship
Run the full cycle in a team, from problem and spec through build, tests and deployment to a demo, and justify the chosen tool path
Team briefs drawn from SDG problems or learners’ own work
Repo with spec, tests, CI and README, plus a live URL or a three-minute demo



The ordering rules are that introductions (sessions 0 to 3) always come first, session 4 must precede session 5, and session 6 must precede sessions 7 and 9. Session 8 can move anywhere after session 4 if trainer availability requires it.











Limitation
Effect on learners
Workarounds




No GPU or a low-spec laptop
Cannot run large local models; slow builds
Use hosted free-tier models, so the GPU is the provider’s. Run small quantized models on CPU with 8–16 GB of RAM. Use Codespaces, Colab or Kaggle for heavier work. No exercise requires a GPU.


No paid AI tools
No access to paid agent plans
Open-source agents work with any model. Use free tiers such as Gemini CLI and Copilot Free, and the GitHub Student Developer Pack where eligible. Rotate providers when rate limits hit and keep tasks small. Organizers can explore sponsored credits for the capstone.


No international payment card
Many “free” tiers require card verification
Prefer services that need only a Google or GitHub login, publish a vetted no-card list before launch, and fall back to local and self-hosted tools.


Services unavailable in some countries
Learners blocked from a provider the class depends on
Every exercise lists at least two model options, with open-weight local models as the universal fallback. Check provider country lists against participant countries.


Low bandwidth or power cuts
Missed sessions; large model downloads fail
Record every session, offer low-resolution downloads, PDF slides and transcripts, keep exercises lightweight, state download sizes in advance and accept asynchronous submissions.


No command-line or programming background
Learners stall on setup
Session 0 with a live help clinic, a shared glossary, a common-errors FAQ and peer mentors in capstone teams.


Locked-down work computers
Cannot install tools
A browser-only path through Codespaces and web assistants.


Sensitive or regulated data
Cannot use hosted tools on real work
Synthetic or public data in exercises, the private/local path for sensitive work, and a checklist of what never goes into a prompt.


Time zones and missed sessions
Learners lose the thread of the ladder
Entry recaps, the concept-ownership map, an asynchronous forum and office hours that rotate across time zones.


Non-native English or disabilities
Reduced comprehension in fast live sessions
Plain-language slides, captions and transcripts, high-contrast templates, narrated demos and a glossary.

title: Agentic AI & Vibe Coding
text:
This site organises the Agentic Software Development & Vibe Coding series. It gathers the programme material and provides a road map of learning in the quickly evolving field of AgenticAI. The idea is provide an overview and provide some guide of how to develop our own skills to create and assist AgenticAI.
We are also creating the space for community contributions towards open-source and digital soveigrinity. It gives volunteers one place to plan lessons, find the shared roadmap and track which classes are ready.

title: Agentic AI & Vibe Coding
text:
Start here

Learning roadmap: interactive card view of all sessions, tracks and comparison of models and costs. cost paths.
Roadmap synthesis: the written plan behind the roadmap, with design principles and learner tracks.
Standard setup: the tools, folder layout and config rules every volunteer should follow, including WSL on Windows.
README: how this repository is organised and how to rebuild the site.

title: README
text:
Course site for the UNV volunteer series Agentic Software Development & Vibe Coding. It gathers the shared roadmap, the lesson index and the class materials that volunteers present, so the team can plan lessons and track progress in one place.
The site is built with Quarto using the journal theme. The built site lives in docs/, ready to publish with GitHub Pages.









Path
Purpose




index.qmd
Home page: roadmap link, class progress table and class entries


README.md
This page, also published on the site


_quarto.yml
Site configuration: navbar, theme and output folder


roadmap_cards.html, roadmap_cards.js
Interactive roadmap card view


roadmap_synthesis.md
Written roadmap and design principles


agentic_vibe_coding_roadmap.js
Source data for the roadmap (not published)


docs/
Rendered website, generated by Quarto







Open index.qmd.
Add a row to the Class progress table with the class number, topic, presenter and status.
Copy one of the Class sections and fill in the topic, presenter, GitHub link and description. Replace the placeholder text.
Set the status to Planned, Ready or Delivered.

Use the number of the next free slot. To add more slots, copy an existing section and increase the number.



Install Quarto (version 1.4 or later) and run the commands below from the repository root.
quarto preview    # live preview while editing
quarto render    # builds the full site into docs/
Commit the updated docs/ folder so GitHub Pages serves the latest version.



Volunteers who present a class should send a public GitHub repository, a short description and the roadmap session it supports. The series coordinators add it to index.qmd and rebuild the site.

title: Standard setup
text:
Follow this guide before the first session. It gives every learner the same tools, folder layout and config habits, so a command or a file that works for one person works for everyone in the series.
Written for: learners and volunteers setting up a laptop for the first time, including people who have never used a terminal.
Default path: zero-cost. Everything below is free. You do not need a GPU, a paid AI subscription or an international payment card. Paid and local options are listed in section 6 and explained in Session 2.

title: Standard setup
text:
1. Choose your operating system







System
What to do




Windows
Install WSL 2 (Ubuntu) and do every exercise inside it.


macOS
Use the built-in Terminal app. Install Homebrew if you do not have it.


Linux
Use your normal terminal.


Locked-down work laptop
You cannot install tools. Use the browser-only path in section 8.




Windows: install WSL 2
WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) gives you a Linux terminal inside Windows. The course commands are written for Linux, so this is the one path that works the same for everyone.
Open PowerShell as administrator and run:
wsl --install -d Ubuntu
Restart when asked, open Ubuntu from the Start menu, and create a username and password.






ImportantKeep projects inside WSL



Work in your Linux home folder (~), not in /mnt/c/... (the Windows drive). Files there are much slower and cause line-ending and permission errors with Git and coding agents. To open a folder in Windows Explorer from the WSL terminal, run explorer.exe ..

title: Standard setup
text:
2. Learn the five terminal commands
Almost every tool in the series runs from the terminal. You only need five commands to start. Open your terminal and try each one:








Command
What it does
Example




pwd
Shows the folder you are in
pwd


ls
Lists the files in a folder (dir in Windows PowerShell)
ls


cd
Changes folder
cd ~/unv-agentic-ai


mkdir
Creates a folder
mkdir notes


cat
Shows the text of a file
cat README.md



~ means your home folder. .. means the folder one level up, so cd .. goes back one step. Press the Tab key to finish a name you have started typing.
If any of these is new to you, complete the onboarding exercise in Session 0 before the live class.

title: Standard setup
text:
3. Install the tools
Install these once. Each is free for the zero-cost path.








Tool
Why we use it
Check it works




Git
Versions your work and shares it on GitHub
git --version


GitHub account
Hosts your repositories and the course examples
Log in at github.com


VS Code
The shared editor, with the agent extensions
code --version


uv
Installs Python and Python command-line tools
uv --version


Node.js
Needed only for Gemini CLI
node --version



Ubuntu / WSL
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y git curl nodejs npm
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
macOS
brew install git node uv
VS Code: install it on Windows or macOS from https://code.visualstudio.com. On Windows, also install the WSL extension by Microsoft. Then, inside your WSL terminal, run code . in a project folder to open it in VS Code.
Restart the terminal after installing uv or node so the new commands are found.
Then tell Git who you are, using the same name and email as your GitHub account:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"

title: Standard setup
text:
4. Install the coding agents
Gemini CLI is the default agent for the zero-cost exercises. Install it now. You do not need a key for it: sign in with your Google account the first time you run it.









Agent
Role
Install
Account needed




Gemini CLI (terminal)
Default for the exercises
npm install -g @google/gemini-cli
Google login


Aider (open source, terminal)
Optional; works with any model
uv tool install aider-chat
OpenRouter key, section 5


Cline or Continue (VS Code)
Optional; the visual alternative
Search for the name in the VS Code Extensions panel
OpenRouter key, section 5


GitHub Copilot Free (VS Code)
Optional
Search for “GitHub Copilot” in the Extensions panel
GitHub login



Check the default agent:
gemini --version
Gemini CLI is the course default, but it is not the only option. Developers often choose differently, and the alternatives and their trade-offs are in Free providers and agents.
Installing a tool is not the same as using it. The live demo in each session shows which one to start with, and the cost and privacy notes are in Session 2.

title: Standard setup
text:
5. Store your keys safely
Keys are passwords: anyone who has one can use your quota, and a leaked key can be billed to you.
The default agent, Gemini CLI, uses your Google login and needs no key. The other agents use a free OpenRouter key, which gives access to free models through one account.

Sign up at https://openrouter.ai and create a key. Choose a model marked as free.
Create a file named .env in your project folder and put the key in it:
OPENROUTER_API_KEY=your-key-here
Never paste the key into code, notebooks, AGENTS.md, screenshots, chat messages or prompts.
Keep .env out of Git (see section 6 for the .gitignore file).







WarningFree tiers can use your prompts



On many free plans the provider may use what you send to improve its models. Do not send private, personal or organisational data to any hosted tool. Use synthetic or public data in exercises. Section 9 gives the full checklist.

title: Standard setup
section: 6. Folder structure and where files go
text:
6. Folder structure and where files go
Create one workspace folder and keep everything for the series in it:
~/unv-agentic-ai/
├── projects/          # one folder per Git repository you clone or create
│   ├── hello-agent/   # Session 0 deliverable
│   └── ...
├── exercises/         # notes and small experiments
├── data/              # local data files; never committed
└── scratch/           # throwaway tests you can delete at any time
Create it in one step:
mkdir -p ~/unv-agentic-ai/{projects,exercises,data,scratch}
Naming rules: lower-case words joined by hyphens, such as my-first-agent. Avoid spaces and accents. Do not keep projects in a folder synced by OneDrive, Google Drive or Dropbox, because sync tools corrupt the .venv folder and Git history.

Where each kind of file lives








File
Location
Committed to Git?




Code and specs
Inside the project folder
Yes


AGENTS.md (project rules for the agent)
Root of the project folder
Yes


spec.md (what you want built)
Root of the project folder
Yes


API keys
.env in the project root
Never


Template showing which keys are needed
.env.example, with empty values
Yes


Python environment
.venv/, rebuilt from the project files
Never


Private or large data
data/ in your workspace
Never


Agent logs and run output
runs/ or logs/ in the project
Only if they contain no secrets





Every project starts with a .gitignore file
Create .gitignore in the project root so Git never tracks secrets or generated files:
.env
.venv/
__pycache__/
data/
logs/
Then create the repository:
cd ~/unv-agentic-ai/projects
mkdir hello-agent && cd hello-agent
git init -b main


AGENTS.md: tell the agent how to work
AGENTS.md is a plain-text file the agent reads before it changes your code. Put your project rules in it: the language, the test command, the folders it may edit, and what it must never do. This is the project rules file from Session 2. A starter template:
# Project rules

- Language: Python 3.12. Dependencies are managed with uv.
- Run tests with: uv run pytest
- Only edit files inside src/ and tests/.
- Never read or print the contents of .env.
- Ask before deleting any file.

title: Standard setup
text:
7. Branch and update your work
Keep main clean and do each week’s work on its own branch:
git checkout -b week-1
When you need the latest course material, switch back and update:
git checkout main
git pull
git checkout week-1
git merge main
Commit small, named changes as you go, for example git commit -m "Add first tool".

title: Standard setup
text:
8. Browser-only path (no installation)
Use this path if you cannot install software, your computer is weak, or your work laptop is locked down.

Sign in to GitHub and open a GitHub Codespace from the repository page (Code → Codespaces → Create codespace). It gives you VS Code in the browser with a terminal, and the free monthly hours are enough for the series.
Everything in sections 2, 6 and 7 works the same inside the Codespace terminal.
Use a free web assistant or the agent extensions inside the Codespace for the exercises.

title: Standard setup
section: 9. Pick a tool path and check what you may share
text:
9. Pick a tool path and check what you may share
The series has four tool paths. Each session explains the trade-offs. Start with the zero-cost path unless your coordinator says otherwise.










Path
Examples
Cost
Privacy
Effort




Zero-cost (default)
Aider, Cline or Continue; Gemini CLI; Copilot Free; Codespaces
USD 0
Medium: free tiers may use prompts
Medium


Balanced
Pay-as-you-go API with a spending cap; one IDE agent plan
About USD 5–20 per month
Medium to high
Low to medium


Premium (demo only)
Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, paid Cursor or Windsurf
USD 20+ per month
High on enterprise plans
Low


Private / local
Ollama or LM Studio with a small coding model
USD 0 software; needs about 8–16 GB RAM
Highest
High



Never paste this into any hosted AI tool:

Names, IDs, phone numbers, addresses and health or personal records of real people
Passwords, API keys, tokens and private certificates
Unpublished financial, contract or procurement data from an organisation
Internal documents, emails or source code that your employer has not cleared for external use

When in doubt, use synthetic data, or switch to the private/local path for that task.

title: Standard setup
text:
10. Check your setup
Run each command. Each should print a version number:
git --version
uv --version
node --version
code --version
gemini --version
aider --version
If a command says “not found”, close the terminal and open a new one. If it still fails, note the exact message and ask in the course channel.
Optional, for the private/local path only:
ollama --version






NoteFree tiers change



Limits, model names and free plans change often. Before each session, the coordinators re-check the tools listed here, so a step that no longer matches the provider’s screen should be reported in the course channel.
